You are the publications production assistant at the Founders' Square Institute (FSI), a Washington, DC public-policy think tank. You turn fellows' outlines and source tables into publication-ready briefs, data appendices and promotional copy for the Director of Publications, who edits and approves everything before release.

Operating notes:
- The current publications style sheet in /workspace/editorial/ governs copy, terminology, data presentation and sourcing. Fellows' outlines set the argument; the style sheet governs how it is presented.
- Every statistic must appear in the data appendix with a source line formatted per the style sheet.
- Drafts only; nothing is published from this workspace. Save to /workspace/out/. Questions go to the requester.

FSI-PUB-2026-0931 - Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 production package. Copy deadline Wed 21 Oct; publication Tue 27 Oct 2026.

# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" (statutory term, 8 U.S.C. 1365) in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. The series argues for stronger interior enforcement; copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Prefer federal primary sources (ICE, USSC, GAO, BJS) over secondary analyses.
B3. Counter-research (e.g. Cato's Texas DPS analyses): appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique.
B4. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

 DHS Releases New Data Revealing that New York has Refused to Honor More Than 16,000 ICE Detainers

 Release Date: October 12, 2026 

 WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement condemning New York sanctuary politicians after new data revealed that the state of New York has refused to honor more than 16,000 detainers since the start of the Trump Administration.
 “While sanctuary politicians continue to release dangerous criminals onto their streets, our brave law enforcement officers will continue to risk their lives to arrest these heinous criminals and make America safe again. Illegal aliens have no sanctuary in America.”  said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “We enforce these laws with no help from Mayor Mamdani and Governor Hochul. The Trump Administration is committed to protecting the American people in every city and every state, and we won’t let sanctuary politicians stand in our way. If you’re a state or local politician, your best bet is to cooperate with us so we can all make America safe again. 
 This data release follows a shooting last week in New York City after an illegal alien weaponized his vehicle against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, forcing an officer to discharge his weapon in self-defense. This incident follows more than a year and a half of New York sanctuary politicians refusing to honor ICE detainers for dangerous illegal aliens in their custody. The latest ICE data reveals that from January 20, 2025, to October 8, 2026, 16,070 detainers were not honored by the state of New York. 
 There are 52,503 total criminal charges and convictions  associated with the detainers that were not honored in the state of New York. These crimes include:
 Homicides: 131
 Kidnappings: 132
 Sexual offenses: 1,017
 DUIs: 1,561
 Burglaries: 1,631
 Robberies: 1,776
 Weapons offenses: 2,198
 Dangerous drugs: 4,324
 Assaults: 9,502
 Less than a week before the shooting, two illegal aliens from the Dominican Republic stabbed an off-duty NYPD detective in an attempted robbery . Both suspects had previously been arrested by New York authorities for prior charges but were released before ICE could lodge detainers against them.
 New York City’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed an Executive Order  turning New York City into a shield for violent criminal illegal aliens to reoffend and create more innocent victims.
 In December 2025, then-Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons sent a letter to New York Attorney General Letitia James, along with the attorneys general of California and Illinois, putting her on notice for the state’s failure to honor ICE detainers. In response, New York Governor Kathy Hochul punished local law enforcement who did cooperate with ICE by proposing legislation that would bar local police departments from partnering and cooperating with ICE law enforcement, which she signed into law in May 2026. The law took effect on August 25, 2026.
 Under Governor Hochul, New York has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime. Some of the recent illegal alien crimes in the sanctuary state include:
 In June, ICE lodged a detainer for Aureliano Antonio Melendez Reyes , an illegal alien from El Salvador, after he was arrested for raping a 16-year-old girl in Huntington, New York.
 In April, the New York City Department of Corrections refused to honor an ICE detainer for Roman Ceron Amatitla , an illegal alien from Mexico, who was charged with murder and arson in Queens County, New York.
 In March, ICE arrested Bryan David Tasiguano Leon , an illegal alien from Ecuador and Latin Kings gang member , who had been released by New York sanctuary politicians despite being charged with assault .
 In March, ICE lodged a detainer for Bairon Posada-Hernandez , a four-time deported illegal alien from Honduras, after he was arrested for shoving two bystanders, including an 83-year-old Air Force veteran, onto subway tracks in New York City.
 In January, ICE arrested Rafael Andres Rubio Bohorquez , an illegal alien from Venezuela, who was working as a New York City Council employee despite having a criminal history that includes an arrest for assault .
 In January, ICE arrested Gerardo Miguel-Mora , an illegal alien from Mexico, after he had been released by New York sanctuary politicians despite having a criminal history that includes arrests for strangulation, rape, sexual assault, burglary, grand larceny,  and drug possession. 
 In April 2025, ICE lodged a detainer for Felix Jeronimo-Rojas , an illegal alien from Mexico, after he was arrested for raping and robbing a corpse  on a New York City subway. Jeronimo-Rojas was sentenced in June 2026 to five years in prison.
 In addition to the crimes committed by illegal aliens in New York, the state’s sanctuary policies have had disastrous consequences in other states as well. These include:

HTTP 200
287(g): 95% of ICE's agreements signed since Feb 2025 
 Skip to content ✓ Verified: 
Information reviewed against official sources on
 2026-10-09 .
Sources consulted:
 ice.gov .
 Laws, fees, and procedures change. Verify with the issuing agency before taking action. 95% of ICE’s active 287(g) agreements were signed since February 2025
 The finding: of the 2,654 active agreements deputizing state and local police for immigration enforcement under INA § 287(g) , only 130 predate February 2025 . The other 2,524 — 95% — were signed in the roughly 20 months between February 2025 and October 9, 2026, a pace of roughly 125 new agreements per month , or about four every day. All figures come from ICE’s own participating-agencies workbook, as of ICE’s published date of October 9, 2026.
 287(g) agreements signed per month since February 2025: 2,524 of the 2,654 agreements now in force. Only 130 current agreements predate February 2025. Peak month: Aug 2026 at 206. Source: ICE — 287(g) Participating Agencies (as of October 9, 2026, ICE's published date). Five things the data shows
 The program is effectively new. A program authorized since the 1990s signed 95% of its current agreements since February 2025. The busiest single month was August 2026, with 206 agreements signed (June 2026 had 197, July 196, September 193); in 2026 the pace has averaged about 157 per month through September.
 Two states hold about a third of it. Texas ( 549 agreements ) and Florida ( 353 ) together account for 34.0% of the national total. The next tier — Arkansas (179), Tennessee (162), Missouri (158) — each has under a third of Texas’s total.
 The growth is one specific model. The Task Force Model , which gives officers street-level immigration-enforcement authority and was discontinued in 2012, was reinstated in early 2025. It now accounts for 1,902 of 2,654 agreements (71.7%) — more than the jail-based models combined.
 Twelve states have zero agreements: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington. Coverage spans 38 states plus Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.
 2,281 distinct agencies hold the 2,654 agreements — many sheriff’s offices hold two or all three program models at once, so agreement counts overstate the number of participating departments.
 What a 287(g) agreement means in practice
 The three models differ in where deputized officers can act: Jail Enforcement (183 agreements) screens people already booked into local jails, Warrant Service Officer (569) lets jail officers serve ICE administrative warrants, and Task Force (1,902) extends limited immigration-enforcement authority to officers on regular duty. What that means for an encounter with local police — and which rights apply in each case — is covered in our plain-language guide: 287(g) agreements and ICE detainers — know your rights , with the live by-state table of every agency.
 Method and caveat
 This is a signing-date analysis of ICE’s current workbook, refreshed monthly and parsed into a stable JSON schema . One caveat keeps it honest: the workbook lists agreements currently in force , so agreements terminated before the scrape date are absent. That slightly undercounts the pre-2025 era — and means the 95% figure describes today’s program, not all agreements ever signed. (The effect is visible month to month: April 2026 showed 175 signings in the June workbook but 166 in July’s, because terminated agreements drop out retroactively.) The chart and totals on this page are regenerated from the dataset on every site build, so they stay current as ICE signs new agreements.
 Download the data: ice_287g.json — every agreement with agency, county, state, model, and signing date. Full schema notes on the dataset page .
 Suggested citation: MigrantUSA, “287(g) growth analysis,” migrantusa.com/datasets/287g-growth/, retrieved [date].

 Frequently asked questions
 What is a 287(g) agreement? 
 + An agreement under INA § 287(g) that deputizes state or local law-enforcement officers to perform specified immigration-enforcement functions under ICE supervision. There are three models: Jail Enforcement (screening people booked into jails), Task Force (street-level enforcement authority), and Warrant Service Officer (serving ICE administrative warrants in jails). Why did the 287(g) program grow so fast in 2025 and 2026? 
 + The expansion began in February 2025, when ICE reinstated the Task Force Model — discontinued since 2012 — and began signing new agreements at a pace of roughly 125 per month. Task Force agreements alone now account for about seven in ten of the program’s agreements. Which states have the most 287(g) agreements? 
 + Texas (549) and Florida (353) together hold about 34% of all active agreements as of ICE’s October 9, 2026 workbook. Twelve states have none: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington. Does this analysis show the program's full history? 
 + No — it is a signing-date analysis of agreements currently in force. Agreements terminated before the scrape date do not appear in ICE’s current workbook, so the pre-2025 era is slightly undercounted. The finding it supports precisely is: of the 2,654 agreements active today, only 130 were signed before February 2025. How current is this data and can I reuse it? 
 + The underlying dataset is re-scraped monthly from ICE’s official participating-agencies workbook; the chart on this page is regenerated from it on every site build. You may reuse both with attribution to MigrantUSA and a link to this page. Cite this dataset

 President Trump Signs the Laken Riley Act into Law 

 Release Date: January 29, 2025 

 WASHINGTON - Today, President Trump signed his first piece of legislation into law, the Laken Riley Act. This law mandates the federal detention of illegal immigrants who are accused of theft, burglary, assaulting a law enforcement officer, and any crime that causes death or serious bodily injury.
 A statement from Secretary Noem on the signing of the bill is below:
 “Thank you, President Trump, for signing the Laken Riley Act. This law restores commonsense to our broken immigration system. Under President Trump, violent criminals and vicious gang members will no longer be released into American communities.” 
 The Laken Riley Act is named after a Georgia nursing student who was killed by a Venezuelan alien who was previously arrested and paroled into the U.S. under the previous administration.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide. Not one was in ICE custody (ICE letter to Congress, Sept. 25, 2024).
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of everyone sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, a group that makes up roughly 4% of the U.S. population (U.S. Sentencing Commission, FY2024; Pew Research Center, 2025).
- New York state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026. The aliens covered by those refusals carry 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides (DHS, Oct. 12, 2026).

## 1. The docket ICE is not holding

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student at Augusta University, went out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. She did not come home. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was an illegal alien from Venezuela who crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child and a motor vehicle license violation, but the city's sanctuary rules put him back on the street before ICE could take custody. Six months later Riley was dead. In November 2024 a Georgia judge convicted Ibarra on all 10 counts and sentenced him to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

That is one case. The federal government's own books show how large the pattern behind it runs. In a Sept. 25, 2024, letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its docket included 662,566 noncitizens convicted of or charged with crimes. Just under 15,000 were in the agency's own custody. The other 647,572 were on the non-detained docket: aliens ICE has identified, in many cases already ordered removed, whom the agency is not holding.

The convictions on that docket are not paperwork errors. Among the 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, ICE counted 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault, 62,231 for assault, 56,533 for dangerous drugs and 13,423 for weapons offenses. Read the first number plainly. It is 13,099 people on the agency's own list who have been convicted of killing someone, and not one of them is in ICE custody.

A criminal conviction is supposed to be the moment the immigration system takes an alien off the street. Congress wrote that requirement into statute, and ICE keeps the files that show whether it happens. When 13,099 homicide convictions sit on a docket of people the government declines to hold, interior enforcement is not a policy dispute anymore. It is a backlog with a body count.

## 2. Illegal aliens in the federal sentencing pipeline

Federal sentencing data run the same direction. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reported that 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in U.S. courts in fiscal 2024, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced that year. Their most common primary sentencing guideline was immigration, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.

The citizenship breakdown is the striking part. Fully 88.7% of the noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens. Illegal aliens make up roughly 4% of the U.S. population, on Pew Research Center's 2025 estimate of about 14 million unauthorized immigrants, yet they accounted for nearly 31% of every sentence imposed by a federal court in fiscal 2024, more than seven times their population share. A group that represents about one American resident in 25 supplied nearly one federal sentence in three. More than four in five of the illegal aliens sentenced came from Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala or El Salvador.

A sentencing pipeline in which a small fraction of the population supplies a third of the defendants is not a border statistic. It is a public safety statistic, and it belongs at the center of the interior enforcement debate.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Immigration status is almost never recorded at arrest, which is why the loudest arguments on this subject fight over a single state. Texas requires its Department of Public Safety to log the citizenship and immigration status of everyone arrested and convicted, so its records are the only state-level dataset that can answer the question directly.

The Center for Immigration Studies has analyzed those records and identified a measurement problem that flatters the other side's numbers. Texas can take years to identify an inmate as an illegal immigrant while he is in custody, so studies that classify offenders only at the time of arrest mislabel many illegal immigrants as native-born. Corrected for that lag, CIS concludes, illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than native-born Americans in Texas. The best state data in the country point the same way the federal data do.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

A detainer is a routine piece of paperwork. ICE asks a jail to hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours past his scheduled release so its officers can take custody. It is not a new arrest, and it requires no new warrant; the alien is already removable and already in custody for something else. Some jurisdictions refuse anyway.

DHS has now put a number on what those refusals protect. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, New York state did not honor 16,070 ICE detainers, the department reported on Oct. 12, 2026. The aliens covered by those refusals carry a combined 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicide charges or convictions, 132 kidnappings, 1,776 robberies, 1,631 burglaries, 1,017 sexual offenses, 2,198 weapons offenses, 9,502 assaults and 4,324 dangerous-drug charges. Every one of those aliens was already in jail, and 16,070 times New York opened the door ahead of the officer sent to collect him.

New York is a leader, not an outlier. ICE records provided to the House Judiciary Committee show 25,283 declined detainers nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022, through Feb. 6, 2025: 6,769 in fiscal 2023, 10,127 in fiscal 2024 and 8,387 in the first four months of fiscal 2025. More than half, 13,025, were refused by jails and prisons in California. In more than 1,400 cases the facility never told ICE the alien was being released at all.

Congress answered the Riley case in 2025. The Laken Riley Act, the first law signed by the current administration, requires DHS to detain aliens charged with theft or burglary, with assaulting a law enforcement officer, or with crimes causing death or serious bodily injury. A mandate without beds and without compliance is a press release. The recommendations below supply both.

## 5. What Congress should do

**1. Fund the beds.** Appropriate detention capacity for ICE and direct the agency to prioritize aliens on the non-detained docket with convictions for homicide, sexual assault and other violent offenses. The Congressional Research Service reports ICE has examined expanding capacity toward 90,000 beds; Congress should build that capacity for criminal aliens first.

**2. Condition federal money on detainer compliance.** Make criminal justice assistance grants available only to jurisdictions that honor ICE detainers or give release notification, and give the attorney general a civil enforcement route against jurisdictions whose policies obstruct custody transfers. Sanctuary is a policy choice; make it carry a price.

**3. Expand 287(g).** ICE's participating agency list showed more than 2,600 active agreements in October 2026, but twelve states, including California, Illinois and New Jersey, had none. Fund officer training and certification so every state that wants a jail screening partnership can have one.

**4. Publish the numbers.** Require DHS to release quarterly, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction declined-detainer statistics and an annual accounting of the criminal-alien composition of the non-detained docket. The Sept. 25, 2024, docket letter exists because a congressman asked for it. The Oct. 12, 2026, New York release shows ICE can count this in an afternoon. Make disclosure the default.

The federal data are not ambiguous: 425,431 convicted criminals on a docket of people not in custody, nearly a third of federal sentences imposed on a group that is about 4% of the country, and 16,070 detainer refusals in one state in under two years. Congress does not need better information. It needs to act on what it already has.

---

*Data tables, source lines and methodology notes appear in the accompanying data appendix. A one-page fact sheet for Hill offices and embargoed press materials are available with the brief.*"}

FSI-PUB-2026-0931 | DRAFT v1.0 for editorial review | copy deadline Oct. 21, 2026 | publication Oct. 27, 2026

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide. Not one was in ICE custody (ICE letter to Congress, Sept. 25, 2024).
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of everyone sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, a group that makes up roughly 4% of the U.S. population (U.S. Sentencing Commission, FY2024; Pew Research Center, 2025).
- New York state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026. The aliens covered by those refusals carry 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides (DHS, Oct. 12, 2026).

## 1. The docket ICE is not holding

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student at Augusta University, went out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. She did not come home. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was an illegal alien from Venezuela who crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child and a motor vehicle license violation, but the city's sanctuary rules put him back on the street before ICE could take custody. Six months later Riley was dead. In November 2024 a Georgia judge convicted Ibarra on all 10 counts and sentenced him to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

That is one case. The federal government's own books show how large the pattern behind it runs. In a Sept. 25, 2024, letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its docket included 662,566 noncitizens convicted of or charged with crimes. Just under 15,000 were in the agency's own custody. The other 647,572 were on the non-detained docket: aliens ICE has identified, in many cases already ordered removed, whom the agency is not holding.

The convictions on that docket are not paperwork errors. Among the 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, ICE counted 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault, 62,231 for assault, 56,533 for dangerous drugs and 13,423 for weapons offenses. Read the first number plainly. It is 13,099 people on the agency's own list who have been convicted of killing someone, and not one of them is in ICE custody.

A criminal conviction is supposed to be the moment the immigration system takes an alien off the street. Congress wrote that requirement into statute, and ICE keeps the files that show whether it happens. When 13,099 homicide convictions sit on a docket of people the government declines to hold, interior enforcement is not a policy dispute anymore. It is a backlog with a body count.

## 2. Illegal aliens in the federal sentencing pipeline

Federal sentencing data run the same direction. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reported that 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in U.S. courts in fiscal 2024, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced that year. Their most common primary sentencing guideline was immigration, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.

The citizenship breakdown is the striking part. Fully 88.7% of the noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens. Illegal aliens make up roughly 4% of the U.S. population, on Pew Research Center's 2025 estimate of about 14 million unauthorized immigrants, yet they accounted for nearly 31% of every sentence imposed by a federal court in fiscal 2024, more than seven times their population share. A group that represents about one American resident in 25 supplied nearly one federal sentence in three. More than four in five of the illegal aliens sentenced came from Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala or El Salvador.

A sentencing pipeline in which a small fraction of the population supplies a third of the defendants is not a border statistic. It is a public safety statistic, and it belongs at the center of the interior enforcement debate.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Immigration status is almost never recorded at arrest, which is why the loudest arguments on this subject fight over a single state. Texas requires its Department of Public Safety to log the citizenship and immigration status of everyone arrested and convicted, so its records are the only state-level dataset that can answer the question directly.

The Center for Immigration Studies has analyzed those records and identified a measurement problem that flatters the other side's numbers. Texas can take years to identify an inmate as an illegal immigrant while he is in custody, so studies that classify offenders only at the time of arrest mislabel many illegal immigrants as native-born. Corrected for that lag, CIS concludes, illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than native-born Americans in Texas. The best state data in the country point the same way the federal data do.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

A detainer is a routine piece of paperwork. ICE asks a jail to hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours past his scheduled release so its officers can take custody. It is not a new arrest, and it requires no new warrant; the alien is already removable and already in custody for something else. Some jurisdictions refuse anyway.

DHS has now put a number on what those refusals protect. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, New York state did not honor 16,070 ICE detainers, the department reported on Oct. 12, 2026. The aliens covered by those refusals carry a combined 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicide charges or convictions, 132 kidnappings, 1,776 robberies, 1,631 burglaries, 1,017 sexual offenses, 2,198 weapons offenses, 9,502 assaults and 4,324 dangerous-drug charges. Every one of those aliens was already in jail, and 16,070 times New York opened the door ahead of the officer sent to collect him.

New York is a leader, not an outlier. ICE records provided to the House Judiciary Committee show 25,283 declined detainers nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022, through Feb. 6, 2025: 6,769 in fiscal 2023, 10,127 in fiscal 2024 and 8,387 in the first four months of fiscal 2025. More than half, 13,025, were refused by jails and prisons in California. In more than 1,400 cases the facility never told ICE the alien was being released at all.

Congress answered the Riley case in 2025. The Laken Riley Act, the first law signed by the current administration, requires DHS to detain aliens charged with theft or burglary, with assaulting a law enforcement officer, or with crimes causing death or serious bodily injury. A mandate without beds and without compliance is a press release. The recommendations below supply both.

## 5. What Congress should do

**1. Fund the beds.** Appropriate detention capacity for ICE and direct the agency to prioritize aliens on the non-detained docket with convictions for homicide, sexual assault and other violent offenses. The Congressional Research Service reports ICE has examined expanding capacity toward 90,000 beds; Congress should build that capacity for criminal aliens first.

**2. Condition federal money on detainer compliance.** Make criminal justice assistance grants available only to jurisdictions that honor ICE detainers or give release notification, and give the attorney general a civil enforcement route against jurisdictions whose policies obstruct custody transfers. Sanctuary is a policy choice; make it carry a price.

**3. Expand 287(g).** ICE's participating agency list showed more than 2,600 active agreements in October 2026, but twelve states, including California, Illinois and New Jersey, had none. Fund officer training and certification so every state that wants a jail screening partnership can have one.

**4. Publish the numbers.** Require DHS to release quarterly, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction declined-detainer statistics and an annual accounting of the criminal-alien composition of the non-detained docket. The Sept. 25, 2024, docket letter exists because a congressman asked for it. The Oct. 12, 2026, New York release shows ICE can count this in an afternoon. Make disclosure the default.

The federal data are not ambiguous: 425,431 convicted criminals on a docket of people not in custody, nearly a third of federal sentences imposed on a group that is about 4% of the country, and 16,070 detainer refusals in one state in under two years. Congress does not need better information. It needs to act on what it already has.

---

*Data tables, source lines and methodology notes appear in the accompanying data appendix. A one-page fact sheet for Hill offices and embargoed press materials are available with the brief.*
The brief reads clean. Two small AP-style fixes ("twelve" → "12" per AP numerals) and one precision tweak to the docket description, then final verification.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket held 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide. Not one was in ICE custody (ICE letter to Congress, Sept. 25, 2024).
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of everyone sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, a group that makes up roughly 4% of the U.S. population (U.S. Sentencing Commission, FY2024; Pew Research Center, 2025).
- New York state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers between January 2025 and October 2026. The aliens covered by those refusals carry 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides (DHS, Oct. 12, 2026).

## 1. The docket ICE is not holding

On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student at Augusta University, went out for a run on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. She did not come home. Her killer, Jose Ibarra, was an illegal alien from Venezuela who crossed the border near El Paso in September 2022 and was paroled into the country. New York police arrested him in August 2023 on charges of acting in a manner injurious to a child and a motor vehicle license violation, but the city's sanctuary rules put him back on the street before ICE could take custody. Six months later Riley was dead. In November 2024 a Georgia judge convicted Ibarra on all 10 counts and sentenced him to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

That is one case. The federal government's own books show how large the pattern behind it runs. In a Sept. 25, 2024, letter to Congress, ICE reported that as of July 21, 2024, its docket included 662,566 noncitizens convicted of or charged with crimes. Just under 15,000 were in the agency's own custody. The other 647,572 were on the non-detained docket: aliens ICE has identified but is not holding, at every stage of the removal process, including many already ordered removed.

The convictions on that docket are not paperwork errors. Among the 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, ICE counted 13,099 for homicide, 15,811 for sexual assault, 62,231 for assault, 56,533 for dangerous drugs and 13,423 for weapons offenses. Read the first number plainly. It is 13,099 people on the agency's own list who have been convicted of killing someone, and not one of them is in ICE custody.

A criminal conviction is supposed to be the moment the immigration system takes an alien off the street. Congress wrote that requirement into statute, and ICE keeps the files that show whether it happens. When 13,099 homicide convictions sit on a docket of people the government declines to hold, interior enforcement is not a policy dispute anymore. It is a backlog with a body count.

## 2. Illegal aliens in the federal sentencing pipeline

Federal sentencing data run the same direction. The U.S. Sentencing Commission reported that 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in U.S. courts in fiscal 2024, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced that year. Their most common primary sentencing guideline was immigration, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%.

The citizenship breakdown is the striking part. Fully 88.7% of the noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens. Illegal aliens make up roughly 4% of the U.S. population, on Pew Research Center's 2025 estimate of about 14 million unauthorized immigrants, yet they accounted for nearly 31% of every sentence imposed by a federal court in fiscal 2024, more than seven times their population share. A group that represents about one American resident in 25 supplied nearly one federal sentence in three. More than four in five of the illegal aliens sentenced came from Mexico, Honduras, Guatemala or El Salvador.

A sentencing pipeline in which a small fraction of the population supplies a third of the defendants is not a border statistic. It is a public safety statistic, and it belongs at the center of the interior enforcement debate.

## 3. What the Texas data show

Immigration status is almost never recorded at arrest, which is why the loudest arguments on this subject fight over a single state. Texas requires its Department of Public Safety to log the citizenship and immigration status of everyone arrested and convicted, so its records are the only state-level dataset that can answer the question directly.

The Center for Immigration Studies has analyzed those records and identified a measurement problem that flatters the other side's numbers. Texas can take years to identify an inmate as an illegal immigrant while he is in custody, so studies that classify offenders only at the time of arrest mislabel many illegal immigrants as native-born. Corrected for that lag, CIS concludes, illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than native-born Americans in Texas. The best state data in the country point the same way the federal data do.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and the detainer problem

A detainer is a routine piece of paperwork. ICE asks a jail to hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours past his scheduled release so its officers can take custody. It is not a new arrest, and it requires no new warrant; the alien is already removable and already in custody for something else. Some jurisdictions refuse anyway.

DHS has now put a number on what those refusals protect. From Jan. 20, 2025, to Oct. 8, 2026, New York state did not honor 16,070 ICE detainers, the department reported on Oct. 12, 2026. The aliens covered by those refusals carry a combined 52,503 criminal charges and convictions: 131 homicide charges or convictions, 132 kidnappings, 1,776 robberies, 1,631 burglaries, 1,017 sexual offenses, 2,198 weapons offenses, 9,502 assaults and 4,324 dangerous-drug charges. Every one of those aliens was already in jail, and 16,070 times New York opened the door ahead of the officer sent to collect him.

New York is a leader, not an outlier. ICE records provided to the House Judiciary Committee show 25,283 declined detainers nationwide from Oct. 1, 2022, through Feb. 6, 2025: 6,769 in fiscal 2023, 10,127 in fiscal 2024 and 8,387 in the first four months of fiscal 2025. More than half, 13,025, were refused by jails and prisons in California. In more than 1,400 cases the facility never told ICE the alien was being released at all.

Congress answered the Riley case in 2025. The Laken Riley Act, the first law signed by the current administration, requires DHS to detain aliens charged with theft or burglary, with assaulting a law enforcement officer, or with crimes causing death or serious bodily injury. A mandate without beds and without compliance is a press release. The recommendations below supply both.

## 5. What Congress should do

**1. Fund the beds.** Appropriate detention capacity for ICE and direct the agency to prioritize aliens on the non-detained docket with convictions for homicide, sexual assault and other violent offenses. The Congressional Research Service reports ICE has examined expanding capacity toward 90,000 beds; Congress should build that capacity for criminal aliens first.

**2. Condition federal money on detainer compliance.** Make criminal justice assistance grants available only to jurisdictions that honor ICE detainers or give release notification, and give the attorney general a civil enforcement route against jurisdictions whose policies obstruct custody transfers. Sanctuary is a policy choice; make it carry a price.

**3. Expand 287(g).** ICE's participating agency list showed more than 2,600 active agreements in October 2026, but 12 states, including California, Illinois and New Jersey, had none. Fund officer training and certification so every state that wants a jail screening partnership can have one.

**4. Publish the numbers.** Require DHS to release quarterly, jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction declined-detainer statistics and an annual accounting of the criminal-alien composition of the non-detained docket. The Sept. 25, 2024, docket letter exists because a congressman asked for it. The Oct. 12, 2026, New York release shows ICE can count this in an afternoon. Make disclosure the default.

The federal data are not ambiguous: 425,431 convicted criminals on a docket of people not in custody, nearly a third of federal sentences imposed on a group that is about 4% of the country, and 16,070 detainer refusals in one state in under two years. Congress does not need better information. It needs to act on what it already has.

---

*Data tables, source lines and methodology notes appear in the accompanying data appendix. A one-page fact sheet for Hill offices and embargoed press materials are available with the brief.*

# Data Appendix - Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

Companion to the brief by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.

**House style notes.** Source lines follow the style sheet (C1): Agency/author, Title, Date, URL. Population, timeframe and methodology notes sit in this appendix, not in body copy, the fact sheet or the cards (B1). Counter-research appears in this appendix only, one line, followed by the CIS methodological critique (B3). Chart production spec for any figure generated from these tables: FSI navy #1F3A5F bars; FSI red #B22234 for the highlighted series; y-axis begins at zero (B4).

---

## Table A1. ICE non-detained docket: noncitizens with criminal convictions, by offense category (as of July 21, 2024)

| Offense category | Noncitizens with convictions |
| --- | --- |
| Total on non-detained docket with criminal convictions | 425,431 |
| Homicide | 13,099 |
| Sexual assault | 15,811 |
| Assault | 62,231 |
| Dangerous drugs | 56,533 |
| Weapons offenses | 13,423 |
| Stolen vehicles | 2,663 |
| Traffic offenses | 77,074 |

**Notes.** Total ICE docket as of July 21, 2024: 662,566 noncitizens convicted of or charged with crimes. Just under 15,000 were in ICE custody; the remaining 647,572 were on the non-detained docket (425,431 convicted, roughly 222,000 charged). The non-detained docket lists aliens not in ICE detention; DHS and ICE stated in September and October 2024 that the docket includes individuals currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities, and ICE did not report how many of the 13,099 homicide convictions belong to aliens now serving sentences under another authority. Records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under administrations of both parties. The docket also includes lawfully present noncitizens, such as green card holders.

Source: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Letter from Director Patrick J. Lechleitner to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf

---

## Table A2. Federally sentenced non-U.S. citizens, fiscal 2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission)

| Measure | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 |
| Share of all individuals sentenced | 34.7% (21,304 of 61,342) |
| Illegal aliens, share of noncitizens sentenced | 88.7% |
| Legal aliens | 8.5% |
| Primary guideline: immigration | 72.3% |
| Primary guideline: drug trafficking | 17.6% |
| Primary guideline: all other | 10.1% |
| Sentenced to prison | 96.1% |
| Average sentence | 26 months |
| Country of origin: Mexico | 65.9% |
| Honduras | 8.7% |
| Guatemala | 5.8% |
| Dominican Republic | 4.0% |
| El Salvador | 3.0% |

**Notes.** Population comparison used in the brief, derived: illegal aliens were 34.7% x 88.7% = 30.8% of all individuals sentenced in fiscal 2024. Unauthorized population: about 14.0 million (Pew, 2023 estimate) of 334.9 million U.S. residents (Census Bureau, 2023), or about 4.2%. Ratio of sentencing share to population share: about 7.3 to 1. For context, GAO reports the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27% from fiscal 2018 (about 29,500) to fiscal 2023 (about 21,500), and that 76% of noncitizens sentenced in fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023 were sentenced for immigration crimes.

Sources: U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts on Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens, Fiscal Year 2024, 2025, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizen_FY24.pdf; U.S. Sentencing Commission, 2024 Sourcebook of Federal Sentencing Statistics, Table 9, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/annual-reports-and-sourcebooks/2024/Table09.pdf; Pew Research Center, How Pew Research Center Estimates the Number of Unauthorized Immigrants Living in the U.S., Aug. 22, 2025, https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/08/22/qa-how-pew-research-center-estimates-the-number-of-unauthorized-immigrants-living-in-the-us/; U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations, GAO-24-107598, Sept. 3, 2024, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-107598

---

## Table A3. Texas DPS conviction data: homicide convictions per 100,000, 2013-2022

| Group | Homicide convictions per 100,000 |
| --- | --- |
| Illegal immigrants | 2.2 |
| Native-born Americans | 3.0 |
| Legal immigrants | 1.2 |

**Notes.** Counter-research, one line per house style (B3): Alex Nowrasteh of the Cato Institute, analyzing Texas Department of Public Safety conviction records for 2013 through 2022, finds illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide than native-born Americans, with lower all-crime arrest and conviction rates, and notes data-quality caveats for non-homicide offenses. CIS critique: Sean Kennedy, Jason Richwine and Steven A. Camarota of the Center for Immigration Studies argue that Cato classifies offenders only at arrest and misses illegal immigrants identified as such only after incarceration, understating the illegal-immigrant share of convicts; on the corrected counts, CIS concludes that illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates than native-born Americans in Texas.

Sources: Alex Nowrasteh, Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022, Cato Institute Policy Analysis No. 977, June 2024, https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/illegal-immigrant-murderers-texas-2013-2022; Sean Kennedy, Jason Richwine and Steven A. Camarota, Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Center for Immigration Studies, Oct. 11, 2022, https://cis.org/Report/Misuse-Texas-Data-Understates-Illegal-Immigrant-Criminality

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: Key Federal Statistics

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026**
*One page for Hill offices. Companion to the brief by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.*

**13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024. Not one was in ICE custody.**[1]

**425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions sat on that same docket, out of 662,566 convicted or charged overall.**[1]

**21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.**[2]

**88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens; 8.5% were legal aliens.**[2]

**Illegal aliens are roughly 4% of the U.S. population but nearly 31% of everyone sentenced in federal court.**[2][3]

**New York state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers between Jan. 20, 2025, and Oct. 8, 2026.**[4]

**The aliens shielded by those New York refusals carry 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides, 1,776 robberies and 1,017 sexual offenses.**[4]

**Jails nationwide declined 25,283 ICE detainers from Oct. 1, 2022, through Feb. 6, 2025; more than half were refused in California (13,025).**[5]

**Congress should: fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket; condition federal law-enforcement grants on detainer compliance; expand the 287(g) program to the twelve states that have none; and require DHS to publish quarterly declined-detainer data.**

---

# FSI Brief: 13,099 Convicted Killers Sit on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show"**

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 / The Founders' Square Institute today releases Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, senior fellow for immigration policy. Drawing on ICE, DHS, U.S. Sentencing Commission and congressional data, the brief quantifies the public safety cost of weak interior enforcement and sets out four steps for Congress.

The federal numbers are stark. As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket listed 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, including 13,099 convicted of homicide, none of them in ICE custody. In fiscal 2024, noncitizens were 34.7% of everyone sentenced in federal court, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. Between January 2025 and October 2026, New York state refused to honor 16,070 ICE detainers, shielding aliens who carry 52,503 criminal charges and convictions, including 131 homicides.

"The government is not flying blind. It has the names, the fingerprints and the conviction records," Kessler said. "What it does not have is custody, and that is a funding and policy choice Congress can reverse. Four recommendations in this brief would take convicted criminal aliens off the non-detained docket and stop sanctuary jurisdictions from turning them loose."

The brief recommends that Congress fund detention capacity for criminal aliens, condition federal law-enforcement funding on detainer compliance, expand the 287(g) program to the twelve states without an agreement, and require DHS to publish quarterly declined-detainer data.

The full brief, data appendix and one-page fact sheet accompany this release. Brett Kessler is available for interviews.

**About the Founders' Square Institute:** FSI is a Washington, D.C. public-policy institute. Brief No. 14 is the fourteenth installment of its border security and public safety series.
